summary: Describes a TLS extension for padding ClientHello messages to a desired size.

eli5.summary: Sometimes a letter needs to be a certain thickness, so you add blank pages. This is blank padding for the first message in a secure connection.

questions: what is the tls padding extension
can a tls server echo the padding extension
subtitle: A TLS extension that pads the ClientHello to a size that avoids buggy server implementations.

tldr.problem: As TLS added cipher suites and extensions, the ClientHello grew, and certain sizes exposed bugs in some implementations.
tldr.mechanism: A new extension type, padding(21), carries only zero bytes, so a client can add exactly as much length as it wants to its ClientHello.
tldr.outcome: A client can steer around size-triggered bugs by growing the message, and the server MUST NOT echo the extension.

today: RFC 7685 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5246. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Pad a ClientHello
sections.content:
Successive TLS versions (see RFC 5246) added support for more cipher suites, and more extensions were defined over time. This made the TLS ClientHello larger, and the extra size brought some implementation bugs to light.

At least one of these bugs can be eased by making the ClientHello even bigger. Since fully patching affected implementations is difficult, this memo defines an extension to pad a ClientHello to a desired size.
sections.eli5: Some old machines choke on messages of certain sizes. Adding blank filler can push the message to a size that they handle fine.

sections.title: The Padding Extension
sections.content:
The new extension type is padding(21), and a client MAY include it in its ClientHello. Its extension_data is an arbitrary number of zero bytes. The smallest padding extension is four bytes long and is encoded as 0x00 0x15 0x00 0x00. A ten-byte extension has six zero bytes of data and is encoded as 00 15 00 06 00 00 00 00 00 00.

The client MUST fill the extension completely with zero bytes, although the data may be empty. The server MUST NOT echo the extension.
sections.eli5: The filler is just a label saying how much blank there is, followed by that many zeros. The server never repeats it back.

sections.title: Example Usage
sections.content:
Consider a client that wants to avoid a ClientHello whose TLSCiphertext.length is between 256 and 511 bytes inclusive, because at least one TLS implementation is known to hang the connection on such a record. After building the ClientHello, the client adds four bytes for the msg_type and length fields of the handshake protocol and tests whether the result falls in that range. If so, it adds a padding extension to push the length to at least 512 bytes.

One edge case: if the original size was between 505 and 507 bytes, the record payload would be 509 to 511 bytes. An extension cannot take fewer than four bytes, so the padding pushes the payload beyond 512 bytes.
sections.eli5: If your message is a bit too thin, add blank pages until it is thick enough. If it is almost thick enough, the smallest blank page still makes it a little thicker than needed.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The padding contents could be used as a covert channel, so they are required to be all zeros. The length of the extension can still be used as a much smaller covert channel.

IANA permanently registered value 21 (padding) in the ExtensionType Values registry.
sections.eli5: Filler must be blank so nobody can hide secret notes in it, though the amount of filler could still send a tiny hint.
